title: GOD COULD HAVE GIVEN MOSES ANY NAME. WHY DID HE SAY, “I AM”?
paragraphs: GOD COULD HAVE GIVEN MOSES ANY NAME. WHY DID HE SAY, “I AM”?

The burning bush was not merely where Moses discovered God's name. It was where a broken fugitive discovered that the God who needs nothing had come looking for people who had nothing left—and thousands of years later, Jesus would speak words that make the fire of Exodus burn all over again.
There are moments when one sentence changes everything.
But before we stand beside the burning bush, we need to remember what kind of man was standing in front of it.
He wasn't arriving from a victory.
He was arriving from a scandal.

Moses had once lived inside Pharaoh's world. Then blood was spilled. An Egyptian died. Moses fled. The man who had once moved through the corridors of power disappeared into Midian and became a shepherd.
Imagine the silence of those years.
The version of your life you thought you were going to live... gone.
Maybe that is why this story reaches places inside us that theology alone sometimes does not.
Because some people reading this know what it means to look at their life and quietly wonder:
The season when you disappointed yourself so badly that you stopped believing God could still use you.
And somewhere along the way, you started thinking your worst chapter had become your identity.
Moses could have believed that too.
But Exodus 3 opens with a shepherd walking through the wilderness.
A bush is burning, yet it is not consumed.
A man who does not yet know what his future is stands before the God who simply is.
God tells Moses that He has seen the suffering of His people in Egypt. He has heard their cries. He knows their suffering. He has come down to deliver them.
Then comes the part Moses probably never expected.
The man with blood in his history.
Moses responds essentially the way frightened people still respond when God calls them beyond the identity created by their failures:
That question is more revealing than it sounds.
Who am I to do this?
Who am I after what I've done?
Who am I after wasting all those years?
Who am I when somebody else is more gifted?
Who am I when my past can still testify against me?
God's answer is stunning because He does not spend the moment rebuilding Moses' self-esteem.
He gives Moses something infinitely stronger.
The heart of the statement is:
Because only moments later Moses asks what he should tell Israel when they ask for the name of the God who sent him.
And God answers with one of the most famous and mysterious declarations in all Scripture:
The Hebrew also allows the future-oriented sense:
“I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE.”
And suddenly God's earlier promise becomes impossible to ignore.
This isn't God handing Moses a philosophical riddle to impress theologians thousands of years later.
This revelation occurs inside a rescue mission.
The point is not that Moses finally possesses a magical pronunciation capable of controlling God.
God cannot be reduced to something Moses can control.
He is not one more tribal deity dependent upon a temple, territory, Pharaoh, human permission, or political empire.
He will be who He will be.
He will accomplish what He purposes.
And Moses' weakness cannot cancel God's presence.
Then God gives the covenant name by which Israel is to remember Him:
Commonly represented in English as YHWH, the four Hebrew consonants traditionally called the Tetragrammaton.
Its precise ancient pronunciation is uncertain, though “Yahweh” is a common scholarly reconstruction. English Bibles have traditionally represented YHWH as LORD in small capitals.
Because Scripture does not present God's name as an abstract vocabulary lesson.
His name is connected with His character, His covenant faithfulness, His presence, and His saving action.
The God speaking from the bush is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
He has not forgotten His promises.
He has not become indifferent to Israel's suffering.
Egypt may have believed Hebrew slaves were disposable.
Pharaoh may have believed himself untouchable.
Moses may have believed his useful years were behind him.
But God had not forgotten any of them.
That is what makes “I AM” terrifying to the proud and breathtaking to the broken.
Moses' failure belonged to his history.
God was already standing in his future.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs that sentence more than they realize.
Your failure exists inside time. God does not become trapped inside the chapter that trapped you.
You keep introducing yourself by what happened.
But those are descriptions of wounds, experiences, sins, consequences, or seasons.
They are not the name of God.
And they do not have the authority to become your final identity when Christ has claimed you.
There is a dangerous counterfeit version of Christian encouragement that says, “Believe in yourself.”
God's decisive answer is not, “Moses, you are amazing.”
Your confidence does not ultimately rest in your ability to become impressive enough for God.
It rests in the God who remains faithful when you are painfully aware of how small you are.
And this is where the road from the burning bush begins moving toward something even greater.
Because centuries later, another scene unfolds.
And Jesus answers with words that have thundered through Christian history:
John tells us what happened next.
This was not received as harmless religious poetry.
Jesus was making an astonishing claim about His identity.
And within the wider testimony of John's Gospel, the connection becomes breathtaking.
The eternal Word was with God and was God.
The invisible God had drawn near.
The One through whom creation came into existence entered His creation.
And now the Gospel forces every reader to confront a question even more important than the question Moses asked beside the bush.
Because Christianity does not ultimately stand or fall on whether Jesus can improve your circumstances.
It stands on who Jesus Christ actually is.
If Jesus were merely a moral teacher, admire Him.
If He were merely a prophet, listen to Him.
If He were merely an inspirational figure, quote Him.
But if the New Testament is telling the truth about Him...
The Gospel is not God shouting motivational advice from heaven.
Jesus Christ entered our broken world.
And at Calvary, the sinless Son of God was crucified.
Human hands drove nails through the hands of the One through whom those hands ultimately existed.
The Creator entered creation and permitted His creatures to crucify Him.
The Holy One bore the judgment sinners deserved.
Then came the silence of the tomb.
But Sunday revealed that death had encountered Someone it could not hold.
And that is why grace is not God pretending your sin does not matter.
Grace walked out of a grave.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
It says your sin was so serious that Christ died—and God's mercy is so astonishing that Christ willingly came to save sinners.
That means the answer to shame is not pretending you never sinned.
The answer to guilt is not learning to love your darkness.
It is bringing your darkness into the light of Christ.
The answer to your scandal is not rewriting history until you look innocent.
It is discovering that Jesus can redeem a history you cannot erase.
Peter had a night he desperately wished he could take back.
Paul carried memories of persecuting the church.
Yet Scripture repeatedly reveals a God whose grace does not merely locate spotless people.
That does not make sin beautiful.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe underneath everything you show people, there is something you have been carrying alone.
Something you confessed but still cannot forgive yourself for.
Something that has made you wonder whether God finally became tired of you.
The God who called Moses from the wilderness is not asking you to save yourself.
Jesus already did what you could never do.
But grace is not permission to remain chained.
Stop negotiating with the sin that is destroying you.
Stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Stop using grace as camouflage for something Jesus died to free you from.
The fear that everybody thinks you are stronger than you actually are.
Because you cannot shock the One who already knew your entire story before calling you.
And you cannot earn the mercy Christ purchased by His blood.
And slowly, sometimes painfully, sometimes through tears and confession and consequences and rebuilding, He begins rewriting what you thought had to be the ending.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Not because Christians become perfect overnight.
He turns rebels into sons and daughters.
The ashamed into people who can finally stop hiding.
The spiritually dead into people made alive in Him.
So perhaps the question tonight is not whether you know that God's name is “I AM.”
Perhaps the question is whether the God who revealed Himself to Moses has become merely information to you.
You can know Hebrew words and still refuse surrender.
You can explain the Tetragrammaton and still hide your sin.
You can defend the deity of Christ online and still refuse to let Christ rule your private life.
You can say “Jesus is Lord” publicly while protecting a locked room in your heart where you behave as though you are lord.
And maybe that is the room He is confronting right now.
Not because He delights in crushing you.
Because He loves you too much to bless the prison you keep calling freedom.
Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another wounded person from giving up tonight.
The friend whose faith is disappearing quietly.
The woman convinced her past disqualified her.
The Christian who has become numb.
The unbeliever who believes Christianity is only about religious people pretending to be good.

Not as a religious performance. Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it absolutely does not. Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Christ, not a reward for supporting a ministry.
There will probably come a night when you need to remember that your changing circumstances never changed the identity of God.
You do not glorify God by purchasing access to Him.
You do not buy His favor.
Christ paid the price for salvation.
Moses stood before the fire and discovered that his weakness was not bigger than God's presence.
Israel stood before the sea and discovered that Pharaoh was not bigger than God's deliverance.
Humanity stood before the cross and discovered that our sin was not bigger than God's redeeming love.
And the empty tomb declared that even death does not get the final word when Jesus Christ enters the story.
remember what God told the trembling Moses:
And when the world asks why you still believe after everything you have been through, point beyond yourself.
The God who hears the cry of the oppressed.
The God revealed supremely to us in Jesus Christ.
The Lord who calls sinners to repent and promises eternal life to those who trust in Him.
Maybe your story really is a scandal.
Maybe there are pages you wish you could tear out forever.
But the glory of the Gospel is not that Jesus finds people who never needed rewriting.
He finds sinners whose stories looked finished—and writes grace where shame thought it had already written the final sentence.
Because when everything else in your life becomes uncertain, there remains One whose identity never trembles:
And perhaps the most beautiful thing about the God who said “I AM” is this:
He already knew every page you would be ashamed of—and He still walked into your wilderness calling your name.
